data:
Caizen is an agent-first attack path analysis system for cloud environments. It collects inventory and findings from cloud APIs, container scanners, and source repositories, builds a graph of the ways an attacker could move between resources, and ranks the resulting paths. Agents query the graph for the context they need to choose a fix and then apply it.
Each edge in the graph records where it came from, when it was observed, and how confident Caizen is in it. Confidence decreases as data ages, and Caizen schedules agents to re-check edges before they become unreliable.
flowchart LR C[Collectors] -->|inventory and findings| B[(Bucket)] A[Agents] -->|evidence| B B --> S[Caizen] S -->|re-check requests| A S -->|context| R[Remediation agents] R --> F[Changes, pull requests, tickets]
data.sections#Sections: Why Caizen The problem Caizen addresses and its approach. Attack Paths How resources and permissions become attack paths. Scoring How paths are ranked. Verification How facts are sourced, aged, and re-checked. Remediation How fixes are prioritized and delivered. Architecture Components and data flow. History The 2024 talk and prototype.

data:
Caizen runs as a single Go service on one VM, with a GCS bucket for storage. Collectors and agents run separately and exchange data with the service through the bucket.
flowchart LR subgraph sources [Sources] G[GCP] CA[Container Analysis] GH[GitHub] end sources --> COL[Collectors] COL -->|raw batches| B[(GCS bucket)] AG[Agents] -->|evidence| B B --> S[Caizen service] S -->|curated data| B S -->|dispatch| AG U[Users and agents] -->|IAP| S
data.agent-dispatch#Agent dispatch: For each edge that is due for a re-check, the service starts a Cloud Workflow that runs the appropriate agent. The agent writes its results to the bucket, and the service loads them the same way as collector data. Agents read the graph only through the service API and cannot modify it directly. Remediation agents use the same API to get the context for a fix.
data.collectors#Collectors:
Collectors retrieve data from GCP, Container Analysis, and GitHub. Most collectors are Cloud Run jobs started by Cloud Workflows.
Each run writes its files under its own raw/ prefix and writes a _SUCCESS marker when it finishes. A Pub/Sub notification tells the service that a new batch is ready.
data.packs#Packs:
Packs contain rules, feed definitions, and agent registrations. Each pack covers one system, such as GCP, GitHub, or a container registry, and consists mostly of SQL.
CI publishes each pack to the bucket under a content hash. The service uses one pinned hash at a time, so rolling back a pack is a configuration change.
data.processing-loop#Processing loop: The service runs a processing loop when a batch arrives and on a timer. Each pass applies the rules, incorporates new evidence, applies confidence decay, scores paths, ranks fixes, and selects the edges that are due for a re-check.
data.service#Service: The service runs as one container on a Container-Optimized OS VM. A single process provides the API, the web UI, data loading, scoring, and agent scheduling. It is the only writer of curated data. Identity-Aware Proxy handles authentication for users and machine clients.
data.storage#Storage:
The service stores all durable state in a GCS bucket. Collectors and agents write their output under raw/, and nothing modifies it afterward. The service derives Parquet files under curated/ from raw/ and can rebuild them at any time.
DuckDB on the VM’s local disk is a cache. Losing the VM causes downtime but no data loss.

data:
These pages describe how Caizen models attack paths, scores them, verifies them, and prioritizes fixes.
Attack Paths Scoring Verification Remediation
An attack path is a sequence of steps that leads from an entry point, such as a public endpoint, to a valuable target, such as an admin role or a sensitive dataset.
data.capability-requirements#Capability requi:
Each edge type defines what an attacker must already have in order to use it, and what it provides.
Edge type Requires Provides Network access Ability to reach the resource Code execution A foothold on the resource Credential access A foothold A credential Data access A credential Access to storage Privilege escalation A credential Administrative control A path must meet these requirements at every step. Network access to a service does not provide that service’s credentials, so a path cannot go from network access to credential access without code execution in between.
data.concrete-and-abstract-graphs#Concrete an:
Caizen maintains two related graphs.
The concrete graph contains the resources in your environment and the relationships between them. This includes projects, service accounts, Cloud Run services, buckets, firewall rules, container images, and repositories.
The abstract graph assigns each resource one or more types, such as compute, identity, credentials, storage, or data, and connects those types with attack path edges. Equivalent conditions on different clouds map to the same abstract edge. A public Cloud Run service and a public EC2 instance both produce an edge from internet to compute. Path finding and scoring use only the abstract graph, so they work the same way for every cloud provider.
Each abstract edge keeps a reference to the concrete resources that support it. Every edge can be traced back to the specific configuration that creates it.
data.data-sources#Data sources: Source Data GCP Cloud Asset Inventory Resources and IAM policies Container Analysis Vulnerability occurrences, and build provenance that links each image to its source repository and commit GitHub Repository settings and access controls Collectors retrieve this data on a schedule. See Architecture for details.
data.example#Example:
The following path is common in GCP.
A Cloud Run service allows unauthenticated requests from the internet. The service’s container image has a remote code execution CVE. The service runs as a service account, and code in the container can request that account’s token from the metadata server. The service account has storage.objectViewer on a bucket that holds customer data. Most teams receive these conditions as separate findings from different tools. A vulnerability scanner reports the CVE, a CSPM reports the public service, and an access review reports the IAM grant. Caizen combines them into one path from the internet to the customer data.
data.latent-paths#Latent paths: A latent path is a path that is missing one edge. For example, a staging service might run the same vulnerable image as production but be blocked from the internet by a firewall rule. Caizen tracks latent paths and flags a path for agents as soon as a configuration change completes it.

data: Remediation agents use the graph to decide which fix to apply first and how to apply it.
data.choke-edges#Choke edges: Many attack paths share edges. A single over-privileged service account can appear in a dozen paths. Caizen ranks each edge by the confidence-weighted value of the paths that pass through it. Removing a highly ranked edge closes every path that depends on it, so agents start with the highest-ranked edges.
data.choosing-an-action#Choosing an action:
An agent working on an edge queries the graph for the context of each resource involved, such as its environment, its owner, and the system that manages it. That context determines the action.
Context Action Sandbox resource Apply the change directly, for example by closing a port with the AWS CLI. Resource managed in Terraform Open a pull request against the Terraform repository. Vulnerable container image Open a pull request that updates the base image. Build provenance identifies the repository and commit that built the image. Change that needs human review Open a ticket for the team that owns the resource. Agents on the receiving teams can handle those pull requests and tickets in turn.
data.confirmation#Confirmation: After a fix ships, Caizen re-checks the affected edges. When Caizen confirms that an edge is closed, it also closes every path that depended on it. This produces an audit trail of which attack paths each change removed.

data: Caizen scores attack paths. A path’s score depends on the value of the target it reaches and the confidence of each step along the way.
data.confidence#Confidence:
Each edge has two confidence values.
Value Meaning Existence The probability that the edge exists Traversal The probability that an attacker who reaches the edge can use it An IAM binding read from the policy API has an existence confidence close to 1. A CVE reported by a scanner can have lower existence and traversal confidence.
data.effect-on-prioritization#Effect on prior: Severity-based tools rank a critical CVE above a medium CVE regardless of context. In Caizen, a critical CVE on a service that cannot be reached produces a low-scoring path. A medium CVE on a public service with an over-privileged service account can produce a high-scoring path. Agents use these scores to decide which paths to work on first.
data.path-score#Path score:
score = value × product over all hops of (existence × traversal) Each hop contributes a factor of 1 or less, so a longer path scores lower unless every hop is highly certain.
In measured examples, most of the uncertainty is in the first hop. One path scored 0.965 × 1.0 × 0.995 × 0.999. The initial access step carried almost all of the uncertainty, and the IAM and metadata server steps that followed were close to certain.
data.unknowns#Unknowns: Caizen also scores missing data. An image running in production that has never been scanned appears as an unknown, ranked by the value an attacker could reach through it. Caizen does not treat it as free of vulnerabilities.
data.value#Value:
Each target has a value. An organization admin role has a higher value than a project role, and a project role has a higher value than read access to a log bucket.
A path’s value is the highest value among the targets it reaches. Caizen does not add values together, because that would give longer paths higher scores only because they pass through more targets.

data: Every fact in Caizen has a source, an observation time, and a confidence that decreases over time. Agents re-check facts in an order set by uncertainty and value.
data.admission-checks#Admission checks:
Caizen validates agent results before accepting them. Each result must be well formed, reference existing resources, describe an edge that is valid between the resource types involved, and come from an agent that is permitted to make that kind of claim.
When an agent finds nothing, Caizen marks the edge unverified. Caizen marks an edge as removed only when it observes a reason, such as a deleted firewall rule.
When agents disagree, Caizen keeps the more conservative value and schedules an immediate re-check.
data.agents#Agents:
Each agent holds credentials for a single domain, such as network probing, source code access, or a container registry. Agents have no direct access to storage. They read the graph through the service API and write their results as evidence, which Caizen loads the same way as collector data.
Caizen treats active testing beyond passive checks as authorized penetration testing and enforces its scope and limits.
data.decay#Decay:
Confidence in an edge decays toward unknown over time. An old observation that an edge existed becomes uncertain. Caizen never treats it as evidence that the edge is gone.
Each edge type has its own decay rate. Network reachability decays quickly. A CVE on a specific image digest decays slowly. When a configuration change affects a resource, confidence in the edges that depend on that resource drops immediately.
data.provenance#Provenance:
Caizen records one of three provenance tiers for each fact.
Tier Source Example Config Read from a cloud API An IAM binding or a firewall rule Agent Observed by an agent A port that responded to a probe Static Reported by a scanner A CVE matched to an image Caizen weights each tier differently and stores the tier with every fact, so an agent can see how each fact was learned. Static findings have the highest false positive rate.
data.scheduling#Scheduling:
Caizen orders re-checks by uncertainty multiplied by the value at stake. Each agent has a budget, and the highest-priority checks run first.
Caizen can resolve most uncertainty cheaply. In one test, re-reading configuration confirmed 22 of 27 edges, and those edges held 13% of the total uncertainty. The remaining 87% was in five edges that passive probes, such as banner grabs and HTTP fingerprints, could resolve.

data:
Caizen began as Pipeline Precognition: Predicting Attack Paths Before Apply, a talk at fwd:cloudsec 2024.
Slides Code from the talk Psychiac, a companion tool that applied the model to Terraform plans in CI
data.the-2024-model#The 2024 model:
The 2024 implementation loaded resources from GCP Cloud Asset Inventory into Memgraph as a graph.
Rules based on MITRE ATT&CK techniques added attack path edges to the resource graph.
The model scored each path by the value of the resources it reached.
Psychiac applied the same model to Terraform plans in CI to show which attack paths a change would introduce before it was applied.

data: Caizen drives agent-first security analysis with a context graph built by and for agents to act on. The usual tool-oriented approach, where each security tool reports its own findings and people connect them by hand, is inefficient and wasteful. It has proven to fall short in large environments, especially against agent-driven attacks.
data.example#Example:
A VM is reachable from the internet, has a CVE, and has an IAM role attached. An agent queries the graph for the VM’s environment, its owner, and what the IAM role can access, and chooses an action right away.
Environment Action Sandbox Close the port directly with the AWS CLI. Production Open a pull request for the DevOps team that updates the base container image, or open a ticket for the security team to reduce the IAM role’s permissions. Agents on those teams can handle the pull requests and tickets in turn.
data.the-approach#The approach:
Most security workflows start with a finding and then go looking for the details around it. Caizen works the other way around. It gathers all security-relevant context ahead of time, and agents keep the graph in sync with the environment. When an agent has to decide which fix to apply first, a few graph queries give it the ownership, environment, and exposure details it needs to choose and act.
Keeping the graph current and re-checking it against reality is tedious, and the amount of work grows quickly with the size of the environment. Targeted agents do this work as well. They keep the graph up to date and keep an audit trail of every check and change.
When a decision needs context that Caizen does not have, the solution is a new collector.
data.the-problem#The problem:
Security tools do not have the context needed to support decisions. Each tool knows only its own findings and nothing about the findings of other tools. Many tools also work from snapshots that go out of date.
To act on a finding, a person looks at it in isolation and then finds the business context by hand: who owns the resource, how critical it is, which environment it runs in, and which regulatory requirements apply. This work is slow, and almost every security team struggles with this in some form.
data.who-it-is-for#Who it is for: Caizen is for cloud security engineers, security team leads, and the platform and infrastructure teams who ship fixes. Each organization deploys Caizen in its own environment.
